213: \begin{abstract}
214:   Many extensions of the Standard Model (SM) predict new neutral vector bosons
215:   at energies accessible by the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). We study an
216:   extension of the SM with new chiral fermions subject to non-trivial anomaly
217:   cancellations.  If the new fermions have SM charges, but are too heavy to be
218:   created at LHC, and the SM fermions are not charged under the extra gauge
219:   field, one would expect that this new sector remains completely invisible at
220:   LHC. We show, however, that a non-trivial anomaly cancellation between the
221:   new heavy fermions may give rise to observable effects in the gauge boson
222:   sector that can be seen at the LHC and distinguished from backgrounds.

231: \section{Introduction: Mixed Anomalies in Gauge Theory}
232: \label{sec:introduction-1}
233: 
234: 
235: It is well known that theories in which fermions have chiral couplings with
236: gauge fields suffer from \emph{anomalies} -- a phenomenon of breaking of gauge
237: symmetries of the classical theory at one-loop level. Anomalies make a theory
238: inconsistent (in particular, its unitarity is lost). The only way to restore
239: consistency of such a theory is to arrange the exact \emph{cancellation} of
240: anomalies between various chiral sectors of the theory.  This happens, for
241: example, in the Standard Model (SM), where the cancellation occurs between quarks
242: and leptons within each
243: generation~\cite{Gross:1972pv,Bouchiat:1972iq,Georgi:1972bb}.
244: 
245: Another well-studied example is the Green-Schwarz anomaly cancellation
246: mechanism~\cite{Green:84} in string theory. In this case the cancellation
247: happens between the anomalous contribution of chiral matter of the closed
248: string sector with that of the open string.\footnote{Formally, the
249:   Green-Schwarz anomaly cancellation occurs due to the anomalous Bianchi
250:   identity for the field strength of a 2-form closed string. However, this
251:   modification of Bianchi identity arises from the 1-loop contribution of
252:   chiral fermions in the open string sector. A toy model, describing
253:   microscopically Green-Schwarz mechanism was studied e.g.
254:   in~\cite{Boyarsky:02}.}
255: 
256: Particles involved in anomaly cancellation may have very different
257: masses -- for example, the mass of the top quark in the SM is much higher than
258: the masses of all other fermions.  On the other hand, gauge invariance should
259: pertain in the theory at all energies, including those which are smaller than the
260: mass of one or several particles involved in anomaly cancellation.  The usual
261: logic of renormalizable theories tells us that the interactions, mediated by
262: heavy fermions running in loops, are generally suppressed by the masses of
263: these fermions~\cite{Appelquist:74}. The case of anomaly cancellation presents
264: a notable counterexample to this famous ``decoupling theorem'' -- the
265: contribution of \emph{a priori} arbitrary heavy particles should remain
266: unsuppressed at arbitrarily low energies.  As was pointed out by D'Hoker
267: and Farhi~\cite{DHoker:84a,DHoker:84b}, this is possible because anomalous
268: (i.e. gauge-variant) terms in the effective action have topological nature and are
269: therefore scale independent.  As a result, they are not suppressed
270: even at energies much smaller than the masses of the particles producing
271: these terms via loop effects.
272: This gives hope to see some signatures at low energies 
273: generated by new high-energy physics.
274: 
275: One possibility is to realize non-trivial anomaly cancellation in the
276: electroweak (EW) sector of the SM. Here the electromagnetic $U(1)$ subgroup is not
277: anomalous by definition.  However, the mixed triangular hypercharge
278: 
279: $\uy\times SU(2)^2$ anomalies and gravitational anomalies are non-zero for a
280: generic choice of hypercharges. If one takes the most general choice of
281: hypercharges, consistent with the structure of the Yukawa terms, one sees that
282: it is parametrized by two independent quantum numbers $Q_e$ (shift of
283: hypercharge of left-handed lepton doublet from its SM value) and $Q_q$
284: (corresponding shift of quark doublet hypercharge). All the anomalies are then
285: proportional to \emph{one} particular linear combination: 
286: $\epsilon = Q_e+3Q_q$.  Interestingly enough, $\epsilon$ is equal to the sum
287: of \emph{electric charges} of the electron and proton.  The experimental upper
288: bound on the parameter $\epsilon$, coming from checks of electro-neutrality of
289: matter is rather small: $\epsilon < 10^{-21}e$~\cite{Marinelli:83,PDG:06}.  If
290: it is non-zero, the anomaly of the SM has to be cancelled by additional
291: anomalous contributions from some physics beyond the SM, possibly giving rise
292: to some non-trivial effects in the low energy effective theory.
293: 
294: 
295: In the scenario described above the anomaly-induced effects are
296: proportional to a very small parameter, which makes experimental
297: detection very difficult. In this paper we consider another situation, where
298: anomalous charges and therefore, anomaly-induced effects, are of order one.
299: To reconcile this with existing experimental bounds, such an anomaly
300: cancellation should take place between the SM and ``hidden'' sector, with the
301: corresponding new particles appearing at relatively high energies.  Namely,
302: many extensions of the SM add extra gauge fields to the SM gauge group
303: (see e.g.~\cite{Hewett:88} and refs.\ therein).  For example, additional $U(1)$s
304: naturally appear in models in which $SU(2)$ and $SU(3)$ gauge factors of
305: the SM arise as parts of unitary $U(2)$ and $U(3)$ groups (as e.g.\ in D-brane
306: constructions of the SM~\cite{Ibanez:2001nd,Antoniadis:02,Anastasopoulos:06}).
307: In this paper, we consider extensions of the SM with an
308: additional \ux factor, so that the gauge group becomes $SU(3)_c \times SU(2)_W
309: \times \uy\times \ux$.  As the SM fermions are chiral with respect to the EW
310: group $SU(2)_W \times \uy$, even choosing the charges for the \ux group
311: so that the triangular $\ux^3$ anomaly vanishes,  mixed anomalies may still arise: 
312: $\ux\uy^2$, $\ux^2\uy$, $\ux SU(2)^2$. In this
313: work we are interested in the situation when only (some of these) \emph{mixed
314:   anomalies} with the electroweak group $SU(2)\times \uy$ are non-zero.  A
315: number of works have already discussed such theories and their signatures (see
316: e.g.~\cite{Antoniadis:06,Anastasopoulos:06,Coriano:07a,Armillis:07a,Coriano:07b,Kumar:07,Antoniadis:07a}).
317: 
318: The question of experimental signatures of such theories at the LHC should be
319: addressed differently, depending on whether or not the SM fermions are charged
320: with respect to the \ux group:
321: 
322: 
323: 
324:  
325:  
326:  
327:   
328: 
329: 
330: 
331: \begin{asparaitem}
332: \item If SM fermions are charged with respect to the \ux group, and the mass
333:   of the new $X$ boson is around the TeV scale, we should be able to see the
334:   corresponding resonance in the forthcoming runs of LHC in e.g., $q\bar q\to
335:   X\to f\bar f$.  The analysis of this is rather standard $Z'$ phenomenology,
336:   although in this case an important question is to distinguish between
337:   theories with non-trivial cancellation of mixed anomalies, and those that
338:   are anomaly free.
339: 
340: 
341: 
342: 
343: 
344: 
345: \item On the other hand, one is presented with a completely different
346:   challenge if the SM fermions are \emph{not charged} with respect to the \ux
347:   group. This makes impossible the usual direct production of the $X$ boson
348:   via coupling to fermions. Therefore, the question of whether an anomalous
349:   gauge boson with mass $M_X \sim 1$~TeV can be detected at LHC becomes
350:   especially interesting.
351: \end{asparaitem}
352: 
353: A theory in which the cancellation of the mixed $\ux SU(2)^2$ anomaly occurs
354: between some heavy fermions and Green-Schwarz (i.e. \emph{tree-level
355:   gauge-variant}) terms was considered in~\cite{Kumar:07}.  The leading
356: non-gauge invariant contributions from the triangular diagrams of heavy
357: fermions, unsuppressed by the fermion masses, cancels the Green-Schwarz
358: terms.  The triangular diagrams also produce subleading (gauge-invariant)
359: terms, suppressed by the mass of the fermions running in the loop. This leads to an
360: appearance of dimension-6 operators in the effective action, having the
361: general form ${F_{\mu\nu}^3}/{\Lambda_X^2}$, where $F_{\mu\nu}$ is the
362: field strength of $X$, $Z$ or $W^\pm$ bosons. Such terms contribute to the
363: $XZZ$ and $XWW$ vertices. As the fermions in the loops are heavy, such
364: vertices are in general strongly suppressed by their mass.  However, motivated
365: by various string constructions, \cite{Kumar:07} assumed two things:
366: \emph{(a)} these additional massive fermions are above the LHC reach but not
367: too heavy (e.g.,  have masses in tens of TeV); \emph{(b)} there are many such
368: fermions (for instance Hagedorn tower of states) and therefore the mass suppression 
369: 
370: can be compensated by the large multiplicity of these fermions.
371: 
372: In this paper we consider another possible setup, in which the anomaly
373: cancellation occurs \emph{only within a high-energy sector} (at scales
374: not accessible by current experiments), but at low energies there remain
375: contributions unsuppressed by masses of heavy particles. A similar setup, with
376: completely different phenomenology, has been previously considered
377: in~\cite{Antoniadis:06,Antoniadis:07a}.
378: 
379: 
380: The paper is organized as follows. We first consider in
381: section~\ref{sec:gauge-invar-chern} the general theory of D'Hoker-Farhi terms
382: arising from the existence of heavy states that contribute to anomalies. We
383: illustrate the theory issues in the following section~\ref{sec:toy-example}
384: with a toy model.  In section~\ref{sec:choic-charg-real} we give a complete
385: set of charges for a realistic $SU(2)\times U(1)_Y\times U(1)_X$ theory. In
386: section~\ref{sec:phenomenology} we bring all these elements together to
387: demonstrate expected LHC phenomenology of this theory.
388: 
389: 
390: 
391: 
392: 
393: 
394: \section{D'Hoker-Farhi Terms from High Energies}
395: \label{sec:gauge-invar-chern}
396: 
397: 
398: In this Section we consider an extension of the SM with an additional \ux
399: field. The SM fields are neutral with respect to the \ux group, however, the
400: heavy fields are charged with respect to the electroweak (EW) $\uy\times
401: SU(2)$ group. This leads to a non-trivial mixed anomaly cancellation in the
402: heavy sector and in this respect our setup is similar to the
403: work~\cite{Kumar:07}.  However, unlike the work~\cite{Kumar:07}, we show that
404: there exists a setup in which non-trivial anomaly cancellation induces a
405: \emph{dimension 4 operator} at low energies.  The theories of this type were
406: previously considered in~\cite{Antoniadis:06,Antoniadis:07a}.
407: 
408: 
409: At energies accessible at LHC and below the masses of the new heavy
410: fermions, the theory in question is simply the SM plus a massive vector boson
411: $X$:
412: \begin{equation}
413: \label{eq:39}
414: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{SM} - \frac1{4g_X^2} |F_X|^2 + \frac{M_X^2}2
415: |D\theta_X|^2  + \CL_{int}
416: \end{equation}
417: where $\theta_X$ a pseudo-scalar field, charged
418: under \ux so that $D\theta_X = d\theta_X + X$ remains gauge invariant
419: (St\"uckelberg field). One can think about $\theta_X$ as being a phase of
420: a heavy Higgs field, which gets ``eaten'' by the longitudinal component of the
421: $X$ boson. Alternatively, $\theta_X$ can be a component of an
422: antisymmetric $n$-form, living in the bulk and wrapped around an $n$-cycle.
423: The interaction term $\CL_{int}$ contains the vertices between the $X$ boson
424: and the $Z,\gamma,W^\pm$:
425: \begin{equation}
426:   \label{eq:59}
427:   \epsilon^{\mu\nu\lambda\rho} Z_\mu X_\nu \p\lambda Z_\rho,\qquad   \epsilon^{\mu\nu\lambda\rho} Z_\mu X_\nu \p\lambda \gamma_\rho,\qquad   \epsilon^{\mu\nu\lambda\rho} W^+_\mu X_\nu \p\lambda W^-_\rho, 
428: \end{equation}
429: We wish to generalize these terms into an $SU(2)\times \uy$ covariant form. One
430: possible way would be to have them arise from
431: \begin{equation}
432:   \label{eq:64}
433:   \epsilon^{\mu\nu\lambda\rho} X_\mu Y_\nu  \p\lambda
434:   Y_\rho\quad\text{and}\quad \epsilon^{\mu\nu\lambda\rho} X_\mu \omega_{\nu\lambda\rho}(A^a)
435: \end{equation}
436: where $\omega_{\nu\lambda\rho}(A^a)$ is the Chern-Simons term, built of the  $SU(2)$ fields
437: $A_\mu^a$:
438: \begin{equation}
439:   \label{eq:90}
440:   \omega_{\nu\lambda\rho}(A^a) = A^a_\nu \p\lambda A_\rho^a + \frac23 \epsilon_{abc} A^a_\nu A_\lambda^b A_\rho^c
441: \end{equation}
442: 
443: However, apart from the
444: desired terms of eq.~(\ref{eq:59}) they contain also terms like $
445: \epsilon^{\mu\nu\lambda\rho} X_\mu \gamma_\nu \p\lambda \gamma_\rho $ which is
446: not gauge invariant with respect to the electro-magnetic $U(1)$ group, and thus unacceptable.
447: 
448: To write the expressions of~(\ref{eq:59}) in a gauge-covariant form, we should
449: recall that it is the SM Higgs field $H$ which selects massive directions
450: through its covariant derivative $D_\mu H$. Therefore, we can write the
451: interaction term in the following, explicitly $SU(2)\times\uy\times \ux$
452: invariant, form:
453: \begin{equation}
454:   \label{eq:48}
455:   \CL_{int} = \bc1 \frac{H^\dagger D H}{|H|^2} D\theta_X F_Y+\bc2 \frac{H F_W D H^\dagger}{|H|^2} D\theta_X 
456: \end{equation}
457: 
458: The coefficients $\bc1,\bc2$ are dimensionless and can have arbitrary values,
459: determined entirely by the properties of the high-energy theory.
460: In eq.~(\ref{eq:48}) we use the differential form notation (and further we omit the
461: wedge product symbol $\wedge$) to keep expressions more compact. We will often
462: call the terms in eq.~(\ref{eq:48}) as the \emph{D'Hoker-Farhi}
463: terms~\cite{DHoker:84a,DHoker:84b}.
464: 
465: 
466: What can be the origin of the interaction terms~(\ref{eq:48})? The simplest
467: possibility would be to add to the SM several heavy fermions, charged with
468: respect to $SU(2)\times \uy\times \ux$. Then, at energies below their masses
469: the terms (\ref{eq:48}) will be generated.
470: Below, we illustrate this idea in a toy-model setup.

480:     \multicolumn{2}{c|}{$\chi_1$} & \multicolumn{2}{c|}{$\chi_2$} \\

506: Consider a theory with a set of chiral fermions $\psi_{1,2}$ and
507: $\chi_{1,2}$, charged with respect to the gauge groups $U(1)_A\times U(1)_B$.
508: As the fermions are chiral, they can obtain masses only through Yukawa
509: interactions with both $\Phi_1$ and $\Phi_2$ scalar fields. $\Phi_{1}$ is charged with respect to
510: $U(1)_B$, and $\Phi_2$ is charged with respect to $U(1)_A$:
511: \begin{align}
512:   \CL_{Yukawa} &= i\sum_{i=1,2}\bar \psi_i \Dsl \psi_i + (f_1v_1) \bar\psi_1
513:   e^{i\g5 \theta_B} \psi_1 + (f_2v_2) \bar\psi_2
514:   e^{-i\g5 \theta_B }\psi_2 \notag\\
515:   &+ i\sum_{i=1,2}i\bar \chi_i \Dsl \chi_i + (\lambda_1 v_2) \bar\chi_1
516:   e^{i\gamma_5 \theta_A} \chi_1 + (\lambda_2 v_2) \bar\chi_2 e^{-i\gamma_5
517:     \theta_A} \chi_2 +\mathrm{h.c.}  \label{eq:12}
518: \end{align}
519: Here we have taken $\Phi_1$ in the form $\Phi_1 = v_1 e^{i\theta_B}$, where
520: $v_1$ is its vacuum expectation value (VEV) and $\theta_B$ is charged with respect
521: to the $U(1)_B$ group with charge $2q_1$, and $\Phi_2 = v_2 e^{i\theta_A}$,
522: where $\theta_A$ is charged with respect to $U(1)_A$ group with charge
523: $e_3 - e_4$. 
524: 
525: The structure of the Yukawa terms restricts the possible charge assignments,
526: so that the fermions $\psi_{1,2}$ should be vector-like with respect to the
527: group $U(1)_A$ and chiral with respect to the $U(1)_B$ (and vice versa for the
528: fermions $\chi_{1,2}$).  The choice of the charges in Table~\ref{tab:toymodel}
529: is such that triangular anomalies $[U(1)_A]^3$ and $[U(1)_B]^3$ cancel
530: separately for the $\psi$ and $\chi$ sector for any choice of $e_i,q_i$. The
531: cancellation of mixed anomalies occurs only \emph{between} $\psi$ and $\chi$
532: sectors. It is instructive to analyze it at energies below the masses of all
533: fermions. The terms in the low-energy effective action, not suppressed by the
534: scale of fermion masses are given by
535: \begin{equation}
536:   \label{eq:1008}
537:   S_\cs =\int \frac{(e_1^2 -e_2^2)q_1}{16\pi^2} \theta_B F_A\wedge F_A +
538:   \frac{(e_3^2 -e_4^2)(2q_2)}{16\pi^2} \theta_A F_A\wedge F_B +
539:   \alpha
540:   A\wedge  B\wedge F_A 
541: \end{equation}
542: The diagrammatic expressions for the first two terms are shown in
543: Fig.~\ref{fig:diagram-triangular-theta}, while the Chern-Simons (CS) term is
544: produced by the diagrams of the type presented in
545: Fig.~\ref{fig:diagram-triangular}. The contribution to the CS term $A\wedge
546: B\wedge F_A$ comes from both sets of fermions.  Only fermions $\psi$
547: contribute to the $\theta_B$ terms and only fermions $\chi$ couple to
548: $\theta_A$ and thus contribute to $\theta_A F_A\wedge F_B$.  Notice that
549: while coefficients in front of the $ \theta_A$ and $\theta_B$ terms are
550: uniquely determined by charges, the coefficient $\alpha$ in front of the CS
551: term is \emph{regularization dependent}. As the theory is anomaly free, there
552: exists a choice of $\alpha$ such that the expression~(\ref{eq:1008}) becomes
553: gauge-invariant with respect to both gauge groups. Notice, however, that in
554: the present case $\alpha$ cannot be zero, as $\theta_A F_A\wedge F_B$ and $
555: \theta_B F_A\wedge F_A$ have gauge variations with respect to different
556: groups.  For the choice of charges presented in Table~\ref{tab:toymodel},
557: the choice of 
558: $\alpha$ is restricted such that expression~(\ref{eq:1008}) can be written in an
559: explicitly gauge-invariant form:
560: \begin{equation}
561:   \label{eq:97}
562:     S_\cs =\int \kappa D\theta_A \wedge D\theta_B\wedge F_A 
563: \end{equation}
564: where the relation between the coefficient $\kappa$ in front of the CS term
565: and the fermion charges is given by
566: \begin{equation}
567: \label{eq:364}
568: \alpha\equiv \kappa = \frac{q_1 (e_1^2 - e_2^2)}{16\pi^2}
569: \end{equation}
570: For the anomaly cancellation, it is also necessary to impose the condition 
571: \begin{equation}
572: q_2=\frac{q_1(e_1^2-e_2^2)}{2(e^2_3-e^2_4)}
573: \end{equation}
574: as indicated in table~\ref{tab:toymodel}.
575: 
576: 
577: The term~(\ref{eq:97}) was obtained by integrating out heavy fermions
578: (Table~\ref{tab:toymodel}). The resulting expression is not suppressed by
579: their mass and contains only a dimensionless coupling $\kappa$. Unlike the case
580: of~\cite{DHoker:84a,DHoker:84b}, the anomaly was cancelled entirely among the
581: fermions which we had integrated out.  The expression~(\ref{eq:97}) represents
582: therefore an apparent counterexample of the ``decoupling
583: theorem''~\cite{Appelquist:74}. Note that the CS term~(\ref{eq:97})
584: contains only \emph{massive} vector fields. This effective action can only be
585: valid at energies \emph{above} the masses of all vector fields and
586: \emph{below} the masses of all heavy fermions, contributing to it.  However,
587: masses of both types arise from the same Higgs fields.  Therefore a hierarchy
588: of mass scales can only be achieved by making gauge couplings smaller
589: than Yukawa couplings.  On the other hand, the CS coefficient $\kappa$ is
590: proportional to the (cube of the) gauge couplings. Therefore we can
591: schematically write a dimensionless coefficient $\kappa \sim
592: ({M_V}/{M_f})^3$, where $M_V$ is the mass of the vector fields and $M_f$ is
593: the mass of the fermions (with their Yukawa couplings $\sim 1$). In the
594: limit when $M_f$ is sent to infinity, while keeping $M_V$ finite, the
595: decoupling theorem holds, as the CS terms get suppressed by the small gauge
596: coupling constant.  However, a window of energies $M_V \lesssim E \lesssim
597: M_f$, at which the term~(\ref{eq:97}) is applicable, always remains and this
598: opens interesting phenomenological possibilities, which are absent in the
599: situation when the corresponding terms in the effective action are suppressed as $E/M_f$
600: (as in~\cite{Appelquist:74}) and not as $M_V/M_f$.
601: 
602: Finally, it is also possible that the fermion masses are not generated via the
603: Higgs mechanism, (e.g. coming from extra dimensions) and are not directly
604: related to the masses of the gauge fields. In this case, the decoupling theorem
605: may not hold and new terms can appear in a wide range of energies (see
606: e.g.~\cite{anomaly-th,anomaly-exp} for discussion).

1221: \section{Phenomenology}
1222: \label{sec:phenomenology}
1223: 
1224: The analysis of the previous sections puts us in position to now discuss the phenomenology
1225: of the $X$ boson.  To do this, we  first detail the relevant interactions it has with the SM gauge bosons. 
1226: 
1227: \begin{figure}[t]
1228:   \centering
1229:   \includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{diagram-vertex-xzz} 
1230:   \caption{$\Gamma_{XZZ}$ and $\Gamma_{XZ\gamma}$ interaction vertices, generated by~(\ref{eq:15})}
1231:   \label{fig:vertex}
1232: \end{figure}
1233: 
1234: The first term in~(\ref{eq:48}) generates two interaction vertices: $XZZ$ and
1235: $XZ\gamma$ (Fig.\ref{fig:vertex}).  In the EW broken phase one can think of
1236: the first term in expression~(\ref{eq:48}) as being simply
1237: \begin{equation}
1238:   \label{eq:15}
1239:   \CL_{XZY} = 
1240:   \bc1 (d\theta_Z + Z) F_Y D\theta_X +
1241:   \mathcal{O}\left(\frac {\partial h}v\right)
1242: \end{equation}
1243: where we parametrized the Higgs doublet as
1244: \begin{equation}
1245:   \label{eq:13}
1246:   H = e^{i (\tau^+ \theta_+(x)+\tau^-\theta_-(x) + (\frac12+\tau^3)\theta_Z)}\left({0 \atop v+h(x)}\right)
1247: \end{equation}
1248: Here the phases $\theta_\pm, \theta_Z$ will be ``eaten'' by $W^\pm$ and $Z$
1249: bosons correspondingly, $v$ is the Higgs VEV and the real scalar field $h$
1250: is the physical Higgs field. 
1251: 
1252: 
1253: The vertices $\Gamma_{XZZ}$ and $\Gamma_{XZ\gamma}$ are given correspondingly
1254: by
1255: 
1256: \begin{equation}
1257:   \label{eq:40}
1258:   \begin{aligned}
1259:     \Gamma_{XZZ}^{\mu\nu\rho}(k_1,k_2|k_3) &= \frac12\bc1\,\sw
1260:     \epsilon^{\mu\nu\lambda\rho}
1261:     ({k_2}_\lambda -{k_1}_\lambda)  \\
1262:     \Gamma_{XZ\gamma}^{\mu\nu\rho}(k_1,k_2|k_3) &= \hphantom{-} \bc1\,\cw
1263:     \epsilon^{\mu\nu\lambda\rho} {k_2}_\rho
1264:   \end{aligned}
1265: \end{equation}
1266: 
1267: Similarly to above one can analyze the second term
1268: in~(\ref{eq:48}). It leads to the interaction $XW^+W^-$:
1269: \begin{equation}
1270: 
1271:   \Gamma_{XW^+W^-}^{\mu\nu\rho}(k_1,k_2|k_3) = \bc2\,
1272:   \epsilon^{\mu\nu\lambda\rho}
1273:   ({k_2}_\lambda -{k_1}_\lambda)
1274: \end{equation}
1275: 
1276: The most important relevant fact to phenomenology 
1277: is that the $X$ boson is produced by and
1278: decays into SM gauge bosons.  We shall discuss in turn the production mechanisms and the decay final states of the $X$ boson and then estimate the discovery capability at colliders.
1279: 
1280: 
1281: 
1282: \subsection{Production of $X$ boson}
1283: 
1284: Producing the $X$ boson must proceed via its coupling to pairs of SM gauge
1285: bosons.  One such mechanism is through \emph{vector-boson fusion}, where two
1286: SM gauge bosons are radiated off initial state quark lines and fused into an
1287: $X$ boson: 
1288: \begin{equation}
1289:   pp\to qq'VV'\to qq'X~{\rm or}~VV'\to X~{\rm for~short,}\label{eq:100}
1290: \end{equation}
1291: where $VV'$ can be $W^+W^-$, $ZZ$ or $Z\gamma$. This production mechanism was
1292: studied in ref.~\cite{Kumar:07}.  One of the advantages is that if the decays
1293: of $X$ are not much different than the SM, the high-rapidity quarks that
1294: accompany the event can be used as ``tagging jets" to help separate signal
1295: from the background.  This production mechanism is very similar to what has
1296: been exploited in the Higgs boson literature.
1297: 
1298: A second class of production channels is through \emph{associated production}:
1299: \begin{equation} 
1300:   pp\to qq'\to V^*\to XV'
1301: \label{eq:1}
1302: \end{equation}
1303: where an off-shell vector boson $V^*$ and the final state $V'$ can be any of
1304: the SM electroweak gauge bosons: $XZ$, $XW^\pm$ or $X\gamma$.  It turns out
1305: that this production class has a larger cross-section than the vector boson
1306: fusion class.  This is opposite to what one finds in SM Higgs phenomenology,
1307: where $VV'\to H$ cross-section is by $\mathcal{O}(10^2)$ greater than $HV'$
1308: associated production. The reason for this is that both vector bosons can be
1309: longitudinal when scattering into $H$, thereby increasing the $VV'\to H$
1310: cross-section over $HV'$. This is not the case for the $X$ boson production,
1311: in which only one longitudinal boson can be present at the vertex. This leads
1312: to a suppression by $\sim (\sqrt{s}/M_V)^2$ of the process~(\ref{eq:100}) as
1313: opposed to the similar process for the Higgs boson.  For LHC energies
1314: ($\sqrt{s}\sim 10$~TeV) this suppression is of the order $10^{-4}$.  Without
1315: special longitudinal enhancements, the two body final state $XV'$ dominates
1316: over the three-body final state $qq'X$, which makes the associated
1317: production~(\ref{eq:1}) about 2 orders of magnitude \emph{stronger} than the
1318: corresponding vector-boson fusion. As we shall see below, the decays of the
1319: $X$ boson are sufficiently exotic in nature that background issues do not
1320: change the ordering of the importance of these two classes of diagrams. Thus,
1321: we focus our attention on the associated production $XV'$ to estimate collider
1322: sensitivities.
1323: 
1324: In figs.~\ref{fig:lep} and~\ref{fig:lhcsigma} we plot the production
1325: cross-sections of $XV$ for various $V=W^\pm, Z, \gamma$ at $\sqrt{s}=14\tev$
1326: $pp$ LHC, $\sqrt{s}=2\tev$ $p\bar p$ Tevatron and $\sqrt{s}=200\gev$ $e^+e^-$
1327: LEP.

1362: \subsection{Decays of $X$ boson}
1363: 
1364: The $X$ boson decays primarily via its couplings to SM gauge boson pairs.  The  important decay channels are computed from the interaction vertices computed above.
1365: The corresponding decay widths are:
1366: \begin{align}
1367:   \Gamma_{X\to ZZ} & = \frac{\bc1^2 \ssw M_X^3}{192\pi M_Z^2} \left(1-\frac{4
1368:       M_Z^2}{M_X^2}\right)^{5/2} \approx \bc1^2\, (45\gev)
1369:   \left(\frac{M_X}{\mathrm{TeV}}\right)^3 +
1370:   \ldots
1371:   , \nonumber \\
1372:   \Gamma_{X\to W^+W^-} & = \frac{\bc2^2 M_X^3}{48\pi M_W^2}\left(1-\frac{4
1373:       M_W^2}{M_X^2}\right)^{5/2} \label{eq:41} \approx \bc2^2\,
1374:   (1.03\;\mathrm{TeV})\left(\frac{M_X}{\mathrm{TeV}}\right)^3 +\ldots\\
1375:   
1376:   \Gamma_{X\to Z\gamma} & = \frac{\bc1^2 \ccw M_X^3}{96\pi M_Z^2}
1377:   \left(1-\frac{
1378:       M_Z^2}{M_X^2}\right)^3\left(1+\frac{M_Z^2}{M_X^2}\right)\approx \bc1^2\,
1379:   (307\gev) \left(\frac{M_X}{\mathrm{TeV}}\right)^3 +\ldots,
1380:   
1381:   ,\nonumber
1382: \end{align}
1383: where $\dots$ denote corrections of the order $(M_V/M_X)^2$. The interaction
1384: term of eq.~(\ref{eq:15}) also allows interaction of the $X$ boson with
1385: $\gamma H$ and $ZH$, which are generically small.
1386: 
1387:  \begin{figure}[t] 
1388:    \centering
1389:    \includegraphics[width=0.5\textwidth,height=0.6\textheight,angle=-90]{c1c2} 
1390:    \caption{Branching fractions of $X$ boson decays into $W^+W^-$ (blue), $ZZ$ (yellow-green) and $Z\gamma$ (purple)
1391: as a function of $c_2/c_1$ assuming $M_X\gg M_Z$.}
1392:    \label{fig:XBF}
1393:  \end{figure}
1394: 
1395: 
1396: At leading order in $M_Z/M_X$ the decay width into $Z\gamma$ exceeds that of $ZZ$ by
1397: \begin{equation}
1398:   \label{eq:55}
1399:   \frac{\Gamma_{X\to Z\gamma}}{\Gamma_{X\to ZZ}} = 2\frac{\ccw}{\ssw}\approx 6.7
1400: \end{equation}
1401: The branching ratio into $WW$ is the largest over much of parameter space where $c_2\gsim c_1$, and  exceeds that of $ZZ$ by
1402: \bea
1403:   \label{eq:57}
1404:   \frac{\Gamma_{X\to W^+W^-}}{\Gamma_{X\to ZZ}}=
1405:   \frac{4}{\ssw}\,\frac{\bc2^2}{\bc1^2} \approx 17.4\frac{\bc2^2}{\bc1^2}.
1406: \eea
1407: This ratio depends on the a priori unknown ratio of couplings $c_2/c_1$. In Fig.~\ref{fig:XBF} we plot the branching fractions of $X$ into the $WW$ (blue), $Z\gamma$ (purple) and $ZZ$ (yellow-green) as a function of $c_2/c_1$.
1408: 
1409: Let us compare decay widths~(\ref{eq:41}) with analogous expressions
1410: from~\cite{Kumar:07}. Schematically, decay
1411: widths 
1412: can be obtained in our case as
1413: \begin{equation}
1414:   \label{eq:50}
1415:   \Gamma_{X\to VV} \sim \bc{1,2}^2 \frac{M_X^3}{M_V^2}
1416: \end{equation}
1417: where we denote by $V$ both $Z$ and $W^\pm$ vector bosons and $M_V =
1418: \{M_Z,M_W\}$.  In case of setup of Ref.~\cite{Kumar:07} the interaction is the
1419: dimension 6 operators, suppressed by the cutoff scale $\Lambda_X^2$. Therefore,
1420: the decay width is suppressed by $\Lambda_X^4$ and the whole expression is
1421: given by
1422: \begin{equation}
1423:   \label{eq:51}
1424:   \Gamma_{X\to VV} \sim \frac{M_X^4}{\Lambda_X^4}\frac{M_X^3}{M_V^2} \frac{M_V^4}{M_X^4} = \frac{M_X^3
1425:     M_V^2}{\Lambda^4}
1426: \end{equation}
1427: The presence of the factor $\frac{M_V^4}{M_X^4}$, appearing in the first
1428: equation of~(\ref{eq:51}), can be explained as follows. The vector boson current
1429: is conserved in the interaction, generated by the higher-dimensional operators
1430: of Ref.~\cite{Kumar:07}. Therefore the corresponding probability for emitting
1431: on-shell $Z$ or $W$ boson is suppressed by the $(\frac{M_V}{E})^4$ where the
1432: energy $E\sim M_X$.  In case of the interaction~(\ref{eq:48}) the vector
1433: current is not conserved in the vertex and therefore such a suppression does
1434: not appear.
1435: 
1436: 
1437: 
1438: \subsection{Collider Searches}
1439: 
1440: Combining the various production modes and branching fractions yields many permutations of final states to consider at high energy colliders.  All permutations, after taking into account $X$ decays, give rise to three vector boson final states such as $ZZZ$, $W^+W^-\gamma$, etc.  The collider phenomenology associated with these kinds of final states is interesting, and we focus on a few aspects of it below.
1441: 
1442: Our primary interest will be to study how sensitive the LHC is to finding this
1443: kind of $X$ boson.  The limits that one can obtain from LEP 2 and Tevatron are
1444: well below the sensitivity of the LHC, and so we forego a more thorough
1445: analysis of their constraining power. Briefly, in the limit of no background,
1446: the Tevatron cannot do better than the mass scale at which at least a few
1447: events are produced. This implies from fig.~\ref{fig:lep}b that $M_X\gsim
1448: 750\gev$ (for $c_i=1$) is inaccessible territory to the Fermilab with up to
1449: $10\, {\rm fb}^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity. The LHC can do significantly
1450: better than this, as we shall see below.
1451: 
1452: 
1453: Moving to the LHC, the energy is of course an important increase as is the
1454: planned luminosity.  After discovery is made a comprehensive study programme
1455: to measure all the final states, and determine production cross-sections and
1456: branching ratios would be a major endeavor by the experimental community.
1457: However, the first step is discovery. In this section we demonstrate one of
1458: the cleanest and most unique discovery modes to this theory.  As has been
1459: emphasized earlier and in ref.~\cite{Anastasopoulos:06}, the $X\to \gamma Z$
1460: decay mode is especially important for this kind of theory. Thus, we study
1461: that decay mode. Consulting the production cross-sections results for LHC, we
1462: find that producing the $X$ in association with $W^\pm$ gives the highest
1463: rate. Thus, we focus our attentions on discovering the $X$ boson through
1464: $XW^\pm$ production followed by $X\to \gamma Z$ decay.

        if missing:

1478: 
1479: One subtlety for this signal is the required separation of the leptons from the $Z$ decay in order to distinguish two leptons and be able to reconstruct the invariant mass well. The challenge arises because the $Z$ is highly boosted if its parent particle has mass much greater than $m_Z$, and thus the subsequent leptons from $Z$ decays are highly boosted and collimated in the detector.  One does not expect this to be a problem for $Z\to \mu^+\mu^-$ decays, as muon separation is efficient. Separation of electron and positron in the electromagnetic calorimeter in highly boosted $Z\to e^+e^-$ final states is expected to be more challenging. We do not attempt to give precise numbers of separability for $e^+e^-$. Instead, we only make two relevant comments. First, one is safe restricting to muons. Second, once separability of $e^+e^-$ is better understood, it can be compared with the kinematic distributions of this example to estimate the number of events that are cut out due to the inability to resolve $e^+e^-$. In Fig.~\ref{fig:3deltar} we show the $\Delta R$ separation of $e^+e^-$ for a parent $M_X=500\gev$, $1\tev$ and $2\tev$.  For example, if it turns out that $\Delta R>0.2 \, (0.1)$ is required, then one can expect about $2/3$ ($1/4$) of the $e^+e^-$ events are cut out by this separation criterion.

 to see what evidence exists for the spin of the $X$ boson. The topology of

  gh    = {ghB, ghWi[1], ghWi[2], ghWi[3]};
  ghbar = {ghBbar, ghWibar[1], ghWibar[2], ghWibar[3]};
  generators = {-I/2 g1 IdentityMatrix[2], -I/2 gw PauliSigma[1], -I/2 gw PauliSigma[2], -I/2 gw PauliSigma[3]};
  doublet = Expand[{(-I phi1 - phi2)/Sqrt[2], Phi[2]} /. MR$Definitions /. vev -> 0]; 
  doublet0 = {0, vev/Sqrt[2]};
  Vectorize[{a_, b_}]:= Simplify[{Sqrt[2] Re[Expand[a]], Sqrt[2] Im[Expand[a]], Sqrt[2] Re[Expand[b]], Sqrt[2] Im[Expand[b]]}/.{Im[_]->0, Re[num_]->num}];

ExpandIndices[ LGhs + If[FeynmanGauge, LGh1 + LGhw + LGhphi,0], FlavorExpand->SU2W]];

LSM:= LGauge + LFermions + LHiggs + LYukawa + LGhost;
